passage:
The mobile tower on the water tank gave Kamal two bars if he stood by the fertiliser sacks, so that was where he read Rhea's messages every night.
Four months of good-mornings. Voice notes in a soft accent from abroad. She called him her gentle farmer.
Tonight the message was different. "Kamal, I'm in hospital after an accident, my cards are blocked. I need 60,000 by morning or they won't treat me. I have no one else."
His hands went cold. He pictured her alone and hurt. The money in the shop account was meant for the monsoon stock. He sent it anyway, at 1 a.m., before he could think.
By morning her number no longer existed.
When Manjula Bhabhi asked at breakfast why he looked ill, he said it was the heat. He couldn't say it aloud, that the gentle voice had never been real. So he reported nothing, and the silence sat on him all day.

qa.q: Where did Kamal stand to get a signal?
qa.a: He stood by the fertiliser sacks, where the tower gave two bars.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when the emergency message arrived?
qa.a: He felt cold with fear for her, picturing her alone and hurt, which pushed him to act before thinking.

qa.q: What could Kamal still do the morning after?
qa.a: He could tell Manjula Bhabhi, report the fraud quickly to the cybercrime helpline and his bank, and remember that being fooled by professionals is not a personal failure.

qa.q: What would change if Kamal had told Manjula Bhabhi at breakfast?
qa.a: He would have support instead of carrying the shame alone, and reporting quickly might give a better chance of help.

grounding: A young man in a small town, after months of online affection, sends shop money for a sudden emergency, then hides the loss out of shame.

passage:
It was 3 a.m. in Vancouver when Yara's voice note came, shaky and breathless. "Chen, they won't let me board without paying a fine. I'm stuck at the airport. Please. I just want to finally be with you."
They had talked every day for five months. She knew his mother's name, his favourite dumplings, the song he sang badly. She had been saving to fly to him. Now, two hours before the flight, this.
Chen opened his banking app. His student loan had just come in. His thumb hovered. If he didn't pay, she'd be alone and scared. If he didn't pay, maybe she'd think he didn't love her.
A small voice asked: why can't she video call from the airport?
He typed, "Video call me, just ten seconds." The reply came instantly: "No time!! Do you want me or not?"
Chen stared at the screen, heart pounding, no longer sure whether this was love or fear.

qa.q: What time was it in Vancouver when the voice note came?
qa.a: It was 3 a.m. in Vancouver.

qa.q: Why did Chen's thumb hover over the banking app?
qa.a: He feared Yara would be alone and scared and that not paying would look like not loving her, so love and fear pulled him towards sending.

qa.q: What protective step could Chen take right now?
qa.a: He could refuse to send money, since the video call was refused, and call someone he trusts and report the account instead of deciding alone at 3 a.m.

qa.q: What does the instant reply "No time!! Do you want me or not?" reveal?
qa.a: It shows pressure and guilt being used to stop Chen from checking, a common sign of a romance scam rather than a real emergency.

grounding: A student, five months into a warm online bond, gets a sudden airport emergency and money request, and love and fear cloud his judgement.

passage:
"Francis, can you lend me ₹30,000? I'll pay you back by next month."
"Deepika, what for?"
"It's Ryan. He's stuck at the airport in Istanbul. His wallet was stolen and they won't let him fly without paying a fine."
"Ryan… the engineer you've been talking to online?"
"Four months. He calls me every night. He's the kindest person I've ever known."
"Have you seen him on video?"
"His camera's broken. But he sent photos."
Francis chose his words carefully. "Deepika, a sudden emergency plus a money request, from someone you've never met, is exactly how these scams go."
"You don't know him!" Her eyes filled. "What if he's really stuck? What if I lose him?"
"Then he'll understand if you ask for a video call first. Right now. Just two minutes."
Deepika stared at her phone for a long time. Then she typed: "Can we video call?"

qa.q: Where did Ryan say he was stuck?
qa.a: At the airport in Istanbul.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when Francis questioned Ryan?
qa.a: Deepika felt defensive and frightened, loving Ryan and scared of losing him if he really was in trouble.

qa.q: What did Francis suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Francis suggested a two-minute video call before sending any money, a simple check a real person would accept.

qa.q: How does Francis see Ryan's emergency?
qa.a: Francis sees the sudden crisis plus a money request from someone never met as a classic scam pattern.

grounding: It shows a young adult in a warm long-distance bond facing a sudden crisis story and money request, her judgement clouded by love and fear.

passage:
I'm Tenzin, and it took me six weeks to tell anyone what happened.
Mira and I met on a language exchange app. She said she was a nurse in Canada. We talked every night for three months. She knew about my exams, my grandmother, my favourite songs. I felt, for the first time, really loved.
Then she wrote that her mother was in hospital and her bank account was frozen. She was crying in the voice notes. She needed ₹40,000 for surgery. I had my scholarship money. I didn't think. I just sent it.
Then another emergency. Then another. After the third, she disappeared.
I was so ashamed. I'm a science student. How could I be so stupid? I didn't tell my parents. I didn't report it.
It was my roommate Anirban who noticed I wasn't eating. When I finally told him, he said, "They do this professionally. You're not stupid." He came with me to the cyber police station the next day.

qa.q: How much did Mira say she needed for surgery?
qa.a: ₹40,000 for surgery.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin keep silent for six weeks?
qa.a: Tenzin felt deeply ashamed and foolish, which stopped any reporting or telling family.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin finally report the scam?
qa.a: Anirban noticed Tenzin wasn't eating, reassured Tenzin that scammers do this professionally, and went to the cyber police station together the next day.

qa.q: How does Anirban see what happened to Tenzin?
qa.a: Anirban sees Tenzin as the target of professionals, not as stupid, and wants to support rather than blame.

grounding: A young adult recalls a warm online bond followed by a crisis and money requests, clouded judgement from love and fear, and shame delaying reporting.

passage:
College counsellor's note, Monday. Written by Rukmini.
Tanvir, final-year student, came in looking exhausted. For five months he has been in an online relationship with a woman who says she lives in Singapore. They spoke every day. He says he has never felt so understood.
Three weeks ago, she told him she'd been in a car accident and needed money for hospital bills before her insurance "cleared." He sent his savings. Then she needed more for a lawyer. He borrowed from two friends.
He said, "I know how this sounds. I'm so ashamed. I couldn't tell anyone." He kept apologising.
I told him that these scams are designed to use love and fear, and that being deceived says nothing about his intelligence.
With his agreement, we reported the profile to the platform and filed a complaint with the cyber police helpline from my office. I have also connected him with the college's financial aid office.

qa.q: What did the woman say had happened to her three weeks ago?
qa.a: She told him she'd been in a car accident and needed money for hospital bills.

qa.q: How was Tanvir feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: Tanvir felt exhausted and ashamed, apologising repeatedly because he believed he should have known better.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take with Tanvir?
qa.a: The counsellor reassured Tanvir it was not about intelligence, reported the profile and filed a cyber police complaint, and connected him with financial aid.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's friends who lent money feel?
qa.a: They might feel worried and possibly frustrated about the loans, but also concerned for Tanvir once they understand he was deceived.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young adult who formed a warm online bond, then sent money after a crisis story, and felt too ashamed to report it.

passage:
Monday, 2 a.m.
Sara says she's in a hospital in Istanbul after a car accident, her wallet stolen, and they won't treat her properly until someone pays. She cried on the voice note. Four months of good-night messages, and she never once asked me for anything, so it feels real.
I almost sent my whole scholarship. My finger was on the button.
Then I remembered Eshaan's face last week when I said she'd cancelled our video call again. He asked, gently, "Has she ever been on camera, even once?" She hasn't. Not once in four months.
I'm so scared she's really hurt and I'm abandoning her. I'm also scared I'm the fool in a story everyone has heard before. The worst part is I'd be too embarrassed to tell anyone either way.
I'm not sending anything tonight. I'm messaging Eshaan now, and in the morning I'll tell Abba too, even if it's awful.
Asif

qa.q: Where does Sara say she is?
qa.a: In a hospital in Istanbul after a car accident.

qa.q: What is Asif afraid of as the voice note sinks in?
qa.a: Asif is scared that Sara is really hurt and being abandoned, and also scared of being fooled, with embarrassment making it hard to tell anyone.

qa.q: What protective steps does Asif choose?
qa.a: Asif sends nothing tonight, messages Eshaan, and plans to tell Abba in the morning, pausing and bringing in trusted people before any money moves.

qa.q: How does Eshaan seem to see the relationship?
qa.a: Eshaan seems concerned but kind, gently asking whether Sara has ever been on camera, a quiet warning without mockery.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a warm long-distance bond who gets a sudden crisis story and a money request, torn by love, fear and shame.
